items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to work with equations of lines not written in slope-intercept form.

Content:
Suppose that we have the following two-variable linear equation:
[MATH: 2x+y-5 = 0]
This equation is, in fact, a straight line equation. But it isn't in the form
[MATH: y=mx+b.]
So how can we determine its slope and [MATH: y]-intercept?

Content:
Using our knowledge of algebra, we can solve the equation for [MATH: y] as follows:
[MATH: 2x + y − 5|= 0; y − 5|= − 2x; y|= − 2x + 5]

Content:
The equation is now in the slope-intercept form [MATH: y=mx+b.] We can now tell straight away that the slope of the line is [MATH: m=-2] and the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: 5.]

Content:
Furthermore, now that we know the slope and [MATH: y]-intercept of the line, we can graph it:

items.title: Converting an Equation to Slope-Intercept Form

key_prerequisites.name: Equations of Lines in Slope-Intercept Form

sections.normalized_html: Find the slope-intercept form of the equation [MATH: 3x-9+12y=6y-9.]
sections.readable_text: Find the slope-intercept form of the equation [MATH: 3x-9+12y=6y-9.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To convert the equation to slope-intercept form, we solve the equation for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \eqalign{ 3x-9+12y&=6y-9\[3pt] 3x-9+6y&=-9\[3pt] -9+6y&=-3x-9\[3pt] 6y&=-3x\[3pt] \dfrac{6y}{6}&=\dfrac{-3}{6}x\[3pt] y&=-\dfrac{1}{2}x }]

Therefore, the slope-intercept form of the line is [MATH: y =-\dfrac 1 2 x.]

sections.readable_text:
Which of the above could be the graph of [MATH: y=mx+b,] where [MATH: m] and [MATH: b] are constants such that [MATH: m \geq 1] and [MATH: b \gt 0?]

[IMG: /graphics/c3dd1f256c19aedbc694a464ce620e41]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that, in an equation of a line in slope-intercept form, [MATH: y=mx+b,]

  • [MATH: m] represents the slope of the line, and

  • [MATH: b] represents the [MATH: y]-intercept of the line.

With that in mind, let's examine the given graph in turn.

  • Graph I is not valid. Notice that the line has a negative slope, which doesn't satisfy the condition [MATH: m \geq 1.] [MATH: \color{red}\times]

  • Graph II is not valid. Notice that the line has the slope [MATH: m \approx\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2},] which doesn't satisfy the condition [MATH: m \geq 1.] [MATH: \color{red}\times]

  • Graph III is valid. Notice that:

    • The line has the slope [MATH: m \approx \dfrac{2}{1}] [MATH: =2,] which satisfies [MATH: m \geq 1.] [MATH: \color{darkgreen}\checkmark]

    • The line has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: b \approx 2,] which satisfies [MATH: b \gt 0.] [MATH: \color{darkgreen}\checkmark]

  • Graph IV is not valid. Notice that the line has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: b \approx -2,] which doesn't satisfy the condition [MATH: b \gt 0.] [MATH: \color{red}\times]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to work with equations of lines not written in slope-intercept form.

Content:
Suppose that we have the following two-variable linear equation:
[MATH: 2x+y-5 = 0]
This equation is, in fact, a straight line equation. But it isn't in the form
[MATH: y=mx+b.]
So how can we determine its slope and [MATH: y]-intercept?

Content:
Using our knowledge of algebra, we can solve the equation for [MATH: y] as follows:
[MATH: 2x + y − 5|= 0; y − 5|= − 2x; y|= − 2x + 5]

Content:
The equation is now in the slope-intercept form [MATH: y=mx+b.] We can now tell straight away that the slope of the line is [MATH: m=-2] and the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: 5.]

Content:
Furthermore, now that we know the slope and [MATH: y]-intercept of the line, we can graph it:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/43fd08fe1846f8db2128e4f1436ae9eb]

---

Item 2 — Example: Converting an Equation to Slope-Intercept Form

Example Prompt:
Find the slope-intercept form of the equation [MATH: 3x-9+12y=6y-9.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To convert the equation to slope-intercept form, we solve the equation for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \eqalign{
3x-9+12y&=6y-9\[3pt]
3x-9+6y&=-9\[3pt]
-9+6y&=-3x-9\[3pt]
6y&=-3x\[3pt]
\dfrac{6y}{6}&=\dfrac{-3}{6}x\[3pt]
y&=-\dfrac{1}{2}x
}]

Therefore, the slope-intercept form of the line is [MATH: y =-\dfrac 1 2 x.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Sketching the Graph of a Linear Equation Given Bounds on the Coefficients
